error_modes.label: MDA control on the localizer-only final

texts.0: SP, due to an unmonitored vertical speed after the FAF, did not level and hold the published MDA on the localizer-only final. The aircraft descended below MDA, which the -0 ft tolerance does not allow, and on one occasion remained more than 200 ft high on the preceding segment. IP intervened with a control input to arrest the descent and re-establish the approach.
texts.1: SP, due to a late transition from the descent to the level segment, did not capture the published MDA within tolerance. The aircraft settled at the +200 ft limit above MDA and drifted at that value until IP verbally prompted the power and pitch correction. The level-off was completed only after the prompt, with no IP control input.
texts.2: SP, due to an imprecise power reduction at the start of the final descent, did not level exactly at MDA on the first attempt. The aircraft stabilized between 100 and 200 ft above MDA, and SP recognized the deviation and returned to MDA without IP prompting or intervention. The descent below MDA was never approached.
texts.3: SP levelled the aircraft accurately at the published MDA and held it within +100 ft with no descent below the minimum. Pitch and power were set in one coordinated adjustment and the level segment was flown to the MAP without oscillation. Altitude control required no prompting.
texts.4: SP flew the descent to MDA with negligible altitude deviation, arriving level at the minimum with essentially no overshoot and no descent below it. The level segment was held steady to the MAP with only minor trim adjustments. Vertical control was consistently accurate throughout.
texts.marginal: SP maintained MDA within standards, but the level-off consistently arrived close to the +100 ft edge before the correction was applied. The trend is a late anticipation of the level segment rather than an inability to hold altitude. SP is expected to begin the level-off earlier so that MDA is captured with margin inside tolerance.

texts_at.1: SP leveled off at the published MDA within the code 1 boundary, settling at the 200 ft limit above the minimum, due to a level-off lead point set for a shallower rate than the descent actually flown. No descent below MDA occurred at any point. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to compute the lead point from the actual rate of descent so MDA is captured with more margin below the 200 ft limit.
texts_at.2: SP leveled at MDA with the deviation settling between 100 and 200 ft above the minimum, due to an imprecise power reduction at the start of the final descent that was corrected only on the next altimeter check. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to reduce power in a single coordinated adjustment so the level-off settles closer to MDA on the first attempt.
texts_at.3: SP leveled the aircraft at the published MDA within 100 ft, due to the power reduction being started a moment after the pitch change instead of together with it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to blend the pitch and power adjustment into one action so the level-off settles without the short lag.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the descent continuing past the level-off lead point and captured MDA at about 150 ft above the minimum, correcting the power setting without prompting or intervention. Starting the power reduction together with the pitch change, rather than a beat after it, would keep even that margin smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good altitude-capture technique.
texts_above.3: SP captured the published MDA within 100 ft on a single coordinated pitch and power adjustment, with no descent below the minimum at any point. The only refinement available was to begin the adjustment a fraction earlier so the level-off settles inside 50 ft. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good altitude-capture discipline.
texts_above.4: SP flew the descent to MDA with negligible deviation, leveling within about 20 ft of the minimum with no measurable overshoot and no descent below it. The technique is already right; only the trim check after the level-off could be marginally quicker. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent altitude-capture technique.

texts.0: SP, due to degraded basic instrument scan after prolonged automated navigation, did not track the localizer with the small heading corrections the approach requires. CDI displacement exceeded 2 dots and the correction applied was in the wrong sense on one occasion. IP intervened on the controls to recapture the localizer course.
texts.1: SP, due to insufficient recent practice in raw-data manual flying, did not damp the localizer corrections and over-controlled the heading. CDI reached the 2-dot limit and remained there until IP verbally called the required heading change. SP recentred the needle only after that verbal cue.
texts.2: SP, due to a heading correction applied later than the needle movement required, did not keep the CDI inside 1 dot throughout the final. Displacement reached between 1 and 2 dots and SP identified the trend and re-established the course promptly without prompting or IP intervention. The remainder of the final was tracked within tolerance.
texts.3: SP tracked the localizer accurately, holding the CDI within 1 dot for the whole final segment. Heading corrections were small, timely and correctly sensed, and the needle was recentred before displacement developed. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP held the localizer needle essentially centred from course capture to the MAP, with deviations barely detectable on the CDI. Drift corrections were anticipated and applied in single small heading increments. Course tracking was consistently precise.
texts.marginal: SP kept the CDI within standards, but corrections were repeatedly applied only once displacement approached 1 dot, so the needle oscillated slowly about the centre. The trend is reactive rather than anticipatory tracking. SP is expected to apply smaller, earlier heading corrections to keep the needle stable near the centre.

texts_at.1: SP tracked the localizer with corrections that damped each deviation before it grew, but CDI reached close to the 2 dot limit on one correction, due to reduced recent practice in raw-data manual flying that left the heading change a beat late. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to start the correction as soon as the needle begins to move so displacement does not approach the 2 dot limit.
texts_at.2: SP tracked the localizer with displacement settling at about 1.5 dots, due to a heading correction applied slightly later than the needle movement called for. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to reduce the interval between needle movement and correction so displacement stays closer to 1 dot.
texts_at.3: SP tracked the localizer accurately, with CDI held within 1 dot for the whole final segment, due to one correction that was sensed a fraction late while attention shifted briefly to the altimeter. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to keep the CDI in the scan through every altimeter check so no correction lags.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the localizer needle drifting toward 1.5 dots and recentred it with a small, correctly sensed heading change, requiring no prompting or intervention. Applying that same correction a few seconds earlier would keep the needle even closer to the centre. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sound course-tracking technique.
texts_above.3: SP held the CDI within 1 dot for the entire final segment, with every correction small, timely and correctly sensed before displacement could develop. The technique is already right; only the very first correction after intercept could be marginally quicker. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to sure-handed course-tracking technique.
texts_above.4: SP held the localizer needle essentially centred from course capture to the MAP, with drift corrections anticipated and applied in single small increments that kept displacement under 0.25 dot. There is little left to refine; the anticipation of drift is already the intended technique. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional course-tracking precision.

error_modes.label: Final approach airspeed control after the FAF

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate monitoring of airspeed during the approach, did not hold the computed final approach airspeed after the FAF. Airspeed departed the +15 / -10 kt band, reaching a value slow enough to require an immediate power increase. IP intervened with power to restore the approach speed.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while attention remained on the course needle, did not maintain the computed final approach airspeed within tolerance. Airspeed stabilized at the +15 kt limit and was corrected only after IP called the speed. No control intervention was needed, but the deviation persisted until the verbal cue.
texts.2: SP, due to a power setting left unchanged after the configuration change, did not hold the computed final approach airspeed inside the +10 / -5 kt band. Airspeed moved into the band between 10 and 15 kt fast, and SP detected it on the next cross-check and returned it to the target without prompting or intervention. The speed remained stable thereafter.
texts.3: SP maintained the computed final approach airspeed within +10 / -5 kt from the FAF to the MAP. Power was set once for the configuration and adjusted in small increments as required. Airspeed control needed no prompting.
texts.4: SP held the computed final approach airspeed with negligible variation throughout the final, effectively on target from the FAF to the MAP. Power changes were anticipated with configuration and trim changes. Speed control was consistently precise.
texts.marginal: SP maintained final approach airspeed within standards, but the indication regularly sat near the fast edge of the band before the power correction was made. The trend is a cross-check interval on airspeed that is longer than the other approach parameters. SP is expected to include airspeed in the scan at a rate that keeps deviations well inside tolerance.

texts_at.1: SP held the computed final approach airspeed with the deviation settling at the 15 kt fast limit, due to an instrument cross-check interval that lengthened while attention stayed on the course needle. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to shorten the cross-check interval on airspeed so the deviation does not reach the 15 kt limit.
texts_at.2: SP held the computed final approach airspeed with the deviation moving into the band between 10 and 15 kt fast, due to the power setting being left unchanged after the last configuration change. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to reset power at each configuration change rather than at the next scheduled cross-check.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the computed final approach airspeed within 10 kt fast and 5 kt slow, due to one power adjustment made a few seconds after the airspeed indication had already started to move. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to anticipate the power change from the configuration itself rather than from the airspeed indication.

texts_above.2: SP detected the final approach airspeed moving into the band between 10 and 15 kt fast and returned it to target with a measured power adjustment, without prompting or intervention. Making that adjustment on the first sign of drift, rather than on the next scheduled check, would keep the excursion smaller still. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid power management on the final.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the computed final approach airspeed within 10 kt fast and 5 kt slow from the FAF to the MAP, with power set once for the configuration and refined only in small increments. The only refinement available is to anticipate the very first power change with the configuration selection itself. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed power management on the final.
texts_above.4: SP held the computed final approach airspeed with negligible variation, staying within about 3 kt of the target from the FAF to the MAP with power changes anticipated at each configuration change. There is little left to refine; anticipated power setting is already the intended technique. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to outstanding airspeed control.

error_modes.label: Compliance with ATC instructions on the approach

texts.0: SP, due to an incorrect read-back that was never reconciled with the actual clearance, did not comply with ATC instructions during the localizer approach. The aircraft was flown on a heading and altitude other than those assigned, and the deviation was not corrected on the controller's repeat. IP intervened to fly the assigned clearance.
texts.1: SP, due to a clearance accepted without confirming the assigned intercept heading, did not comply with the ATC instruction as issued. The aircraft was flown through the assigned heading and reached the tolerance limits before the controller queried the deviation. SP corrected only after IP verbally directed the assigned values.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed action on the descent clearance, did not comply with the ATC instruction at the point it was issued. The aircraft remained above the cleared altitude for a short period within the code 1 band, and SP recognized the omission and complied without prompting or intervention. Subsequent instructions were actioned on receipt.
texts.3: SP complied with all ATC instructions on the localizer approach, reading back correctly and flying the assigned headings, altitudes and speeds when issued. Clearances were actioned promptly and the approach clearance was accepted at the correct point. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP anticipated and complied with every ATC instruction with no delay, and read-backs were complete and accurate. Assigned parameters were established immediately and confirmed against the approach plate. Coordination with the controller was consistently accurate throughout.
texts.marginal: SP complied with ATC instructions within standards, but action on each clearance came only after a noticeable pause and one read-back needed a controller correction. The trend is late assimilation of instructions during high cockpit workload. SP is expected to read back accurately and action clearances without delay.

texts_at.1: SP complied with the ATC instructions on the localizer approach, with one descent clearance actioned only after the controller's repeat, due to a clearance accepted without confirming the assigned altitude against the approach plate. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to confirm each clearance against the plate on receipt so no instruction needs a repeat.
texts_at.2: SP complied with the ATC instructions on the localizer approach, with one heading correction actioned a few seconds after it was issued, due to attention held on the approach setup at the moment the instruction was transmitted. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to keep a listening watch active through the setup so instructions are actioned on receipt.
texts_at.3: SP complied with every ATC instruction on the localizer approach, reading back correctly and flying the assigned values, with one read-back slightly slow while the approach was being briefed to the other seat. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to separate the read-back from the briefing so both are delivered without competing for the same moment.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the delay on the descent clearance and actioned it ahead of a controller repeat, correcting the omission without prompting or intervention. Confirming each clearance against the plate the moment it is issued would remove even that short delay. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady radio discipline on the approach.
texts_above.3: SP complied with every ATC instruction on the localizer approach without delay, reading back correctly and flying each assigned value as it was issued. The only refinement available is to fold the plate confirmation into the same breath as the read-back. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to consistently accurate compliance.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated and complied with every ATC instruction with no delay, and every read-back was complete and accurate on first transmission. There is little left to refine; the coordination with the controller is already the intended standard. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary radio discipline on the approach.

error_modes.label: Routing and altitude restrictions (MAIP / Instrument Approach Manuals)

texts.0: SP, due to a published approach plate that was not reviewed before commencing the approach, did not observe the routing and altitude restrictions in the MAIP and Instrument Approach Manuals. A step-down altitude was flown below the published minimum on the intermediate segment, and the course was flown outside the depicted routing. IP intervened to restore the published profile.
texts.1: SP, due to a step-down fix that was not identified in the descent planning, did not respect the published altitude restriction at that fix. The aircraft arrived at the restriction at the code 1 limit and the profile was regained only after IP called the published altitude. The remainder of the approach followed the published routing.
texts.2: SP, due to a descent rate that was not adjusted for the distance remaining, did not meet the published step-down altitude exactly at the fix. The deviation stayed in the band between code 3 and code 1 and SP corrected the profile before the next segment without prompting or intervention. No published restriction was violated.
texts.3: SP flew the localizer approach on the published routing and met every altitude restriction of the MAIP and Instrument Approach Manuals. The step-down profile was planned before the FAF and flown accurately to MDA. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP flew the published routing and altitude restrictions with negligible deviation, arriving at each fix at the correct altitude and track. Descent planning was completed early and the profile required no adjustment. Compliance with the published approach was consistently accurate.
texts.marginal: SP respected the published routing and altitude restrictions within standards, but arrivals at the step-down fixes were repeatedly close to the tolerance edge. The trend is descent planning done fix by fix rather than for the whole profile. SP is expected to plan the descent so that each published altitude is met with margin.

texts_at.1: SP observed the routing and altitude restrictions of the MAIP on the localizer approach, with the step-down altitude met only at the code 1 limit of the tolerance, due to the descent planning being done fix by fix rather than for the whole profile. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to plan the full step-down profile before the FAF so each restriction is met with more margin.
texts_at.2: SP observed the published routing and altitude restrictions, with one step-down altitude met inside the code 2 band of the tolerance, due to a descent rate that was not adjusted for the distance remaining to the fix. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to compute the descent rate from the distance to each fix rather than adjusting it once the fix is close.
texts_at.3: SP flew the localizer approach on the published routing and met every altitude restriction of the MAIP, with the step-down profile planned before the FAF, due to one segment where the planned rate needed a small correction on the descent to the next fix. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to check the planned rate against the actual one earlier in each segment.

texts_above.2: SP identified the step-down restriction before it was infringed and climbed back to the correct profile without prompting or intervention, keeping the deviation inside the code 2 band of the published tolerance. Comparing the descent rate against the distance to the fix earlier in the segment would remove the need for that correction. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to dependable descent planning.
texts_above.3: SP flew the localizer approach on the published routing and met every altitude restriction with the profile planned before the FAF, so no restriction was approached from below at any point. The only refinement available is to build the same margin into the very first segment as into the later ones. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good descent planning.
texts_above.4: SP observed every published routing and altitude restriction with a comfortable margin at each fix, quoting the applicable limits from the briefing without hesitation. There is little left to refine; the descent is already planned for the whole profile rather than fix by fix. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior descent planning.

error_modes.label: Execution of the localizer-only procedure sequence

texts.0: SP, due to an approach sequence executed from memory instead of the published procedure, did not execute the localizer-only final IAW AFMAN 11-202 VOL3, the Flight Manuals and the Techniques and Procedures Manual. Approach mode selection and identification of the localizer were omitted, and the descent was started without the FAF being identified. IP intervened to re-establish the correct sequence.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete review of the approach plate during the setup, did not execute the procedure without mistakes. The navigation aid was tuned but not identified and the timing was not started at the FAF, and both items were completed only after IP verbally prompted them. No control intervention was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a setup begun later than the workload allowed, did not complete the approach sequence in the standardized order. Two items were performed out of sequence and SP recognized the omission and completed them before the FAF without prompting or intervention. The approach itself was flown as published.
texts.3: SP executed the localizer-only approach in accordance with the standardized procedures of AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 and the Flight Manuals, with the aid tuned and identified, the approach set up before the intercept and timing started at the FAF. The sequence was completed without mistakes and without IP intervention.
texts.4: SP executed the full localizer-only sequence flawlessly, with the setup complete well before the intercept and every step performed in the correct order. Cockpit organization left capacity available for aircraft control throughout the approach. No item required prompting at any stage.
texts.marginal: SP executed the procedure to standard, but the setup was consistently completed only just before the intercept, leaving little margin for a late change. The trend is compressed approach preparation rather than incorrect procedure. SP is expected to complete the setup and identification earlier so the final can be flown with spare capacity.

texts_at.1: SP executed the localizer-only approach sequence with the navigation aid tuned and identified only after the timing had already started at the FAF, due to an approach plate review that was completed later than the setup allowed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to complete the plate review early enough that identification precedes the FAF rather than following it.
texts_at.2: SP executed the approach sequence in standardized order, with one item completed a few seconds after the standard point in the sequence, due to the setup being started later than the workload of the intercept allowed. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to begin the setup at the same point on every approach regardless of the workload leading into it.
texts_at.3: SP executed the localizer-only approach in accordance with the standardized procedures, with the aid tuned and identified and timing started at the FAF, due to the setup being completed only just before the intercept rather than well before it. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to move the setup earlier so it is complete with margin before the intercept.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the two items performed out of the standardized sequence and completed them before the FAF without prompting or intervention, so the approach itself was flown as published. Starting the setup at the same point on every approach, rather than only when workload allows, would prevent the sequence slipping in the first place. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured procedural discipline.
texts_above.3: SP executed the localizer-only approach in accordance with the standardized procedures, with the aid tuned and identified and the sequence completed without mistakes or intervention. The only refinement available is to complete the setup with more margin before the intercept rather than at the last usable point. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise procedural discipline.
texts_above.4: SP executed the full localizer-only sequence flawlessly, with the setup complete well before the intercept and every step performed in the correct order, leaving spare capacity for aircraft control throughout the approach. There is little left to refine; the sequence is already ahead of the aircraft rather than reacting to it. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to first-rate procedural discipline.

error_modes.label: Configuration and timing management to the MAP

texts.0: SP, due to a configuration change made without reference to the checklist, did not manage the final approach configuration and timing as required for a localizer-only approach. The aircraft reached MDA in an incorrect configuration and the timing to the MAP was neither started nor reconstructed, so the MAP could not be identified. IP intervened to configure the aircraft and identify the missed approach point.
texts.1: SP, due to attention held on the course needle during the configuration change, did not configure and start timing at the published point. Gear and flaps were selected late and the timing was started only after IP called it, which left the MAP identification dependent on the prompt. Aircraft control remained with SP throughout.
texts.2: SP, due to a configuration change initiated after the FAF rather than before it, did not have the aircraft fully stabilized at the start of the final segment. Airspeed and altitude moved inside the code 1 band during the change and SP restored both and confirmed the timing without prompting or intervention. The MAP was identified correctly.
texts.3: SP configured the aircraft at the correct point, started the timing at the FAF and identified the MAP accurately on the localizer-only approach. The aircraft was stable in the final configuration before the descent to MDA. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP managed configuration and timing with negligible variation, with the aircraft stable in the landing configuration well before the FAF and the MAP identified precisely. Each action was anticipated and required no adjustment. Cockpit management was consistently accurate to the MAP.
texts.marginal: SP managed configuration and timing within standards, but the changes were repeatedly made at the last usable point before the FAF. The trend is task stacking at the start of the final segment. SP is expected to configure earlier so that the aircraft is stable before the descent to MDA begins.

texts_at.1: SP configured the aircraft and started the timing at the FAF with the MAP identification depending on the timing being confirmed a second time, due to attention held on the course needle during the configuration change. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to confirm the timing start at the moment gear and flaps are selected rather than afterward.
texts_at.2: SP configured the aircraft and started the timing at the correct points, with the configuration change initiated a few seconds after the FAF rather than before it, due to the aircraft not yet being fully stabilized at the start of the final segment. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to begin the configuration change before the FAF so the final segment starts already stabilized.
texts_at.3: SP configured the aircraft at the correct point, started timing at the FAF and identified the MAP accurately, due to the configuration change being made at the earliest usable point rather than with a working margin ahead of it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to bring the configuration point forward so a working margin exists ahead of the descent to MDA.

texts_above.2: SP restored airspeed and altitude after the configuration change initiated after the FAF and confirmed the timing without prompting or intervention, with the MAP identified correctly. Beginning the configuration change before the FAF, rather than restoring the parameters afterward, would remove the excursion entirely. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to competent configuration management.
texts_above.3: SP configured the aircraft at the correct point, started the timing at the FAF and identified the MAP accurately, with the aircraft stable in the final configuration before the descent to MDA began. The only refinement available is to build the same margin ahead of every configuration change rather than only the later ones. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to disciplined configuration management.
texts_above.4: SP managed configuration and timing with negligible variation, with the aircraft stable in the landing configuration well before the FAF and the MAP identified precisely on the first check. There is little left to refine; each action is already anticipated rather than reacted to. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless configuration management.

error_modes.label: Decision at the MAP and transition to the missed approach

texts.0: SP, due to continuation bias in maintaining the approach after the conditions had deteriorated below the briefed minima, did not execute the missed approach at the MAP with the required visual references absent. The aircraft was flown below MDA past the MAP, which the -0 ft tolerance does not permit. IP intervened on the controls to initiate the missed approach.
texts.1: SP, due to continuation of the plan after the information that invalidated it had already been received, did not decide at the MAP within the time available. The aircraft remained at MDA past the MAP and the go-around was initiated only after IP verbally directed it. The subsequent missed approach was flown by SP without control intervention.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed assessment of the visual references at the minimum, did not initiate the missed approach exactly at the MAP. The go-around was started slightly late with altitude staying inside the code 1 band and no descent below MDA, and SP recognized the point and acted without prompting or intervention. The published missed approach was then flown correctly.
texts.3: SP made a timely decision at the MAP, initiated the missed approach at the published point with the correct pitch, power and configuration sequence, and did not descend below MDA. The published missed approach routing and altitude were followed accurately. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP identified the MAP precisely and transitioned to the missed approach with negligible delay, establishing the climb and configuration in one smooth sequence. The published missed approach was flown accurately with the aircraft never below MDA. The decision and execution were consistently sound.
texts.marginal: SP decided at the MAP within standards, but the decision was consistently made at the last available moment and the go-around initiation was abrupt. The trend is a bias toward continuing rather than an unwillingness to go around. SP is expected to assess the references earlier and commit to the missed approach decision at the MAP without hesitation.

texts_at.1: SP decided at the MAP with the go-around initiated only after the aircraft had remained at MDA for a few seconds past the point, due to the assessment of the visual references being started later than the approach to minima allowed. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to begin assessing the references earlier on the final segment so the decision is ready at the MAP itself.
texts_at.2: SP initiated the missed approach slightly late against the published point, with altitude staying inside the code 2 band of the tolerance and no descent below MDA, due to a delayed assessment of the visual references at the minimum. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to complete the reference assessment a few seconds earlier so the decision coincides with reaching the MAP.
texts_at.3: SP made a timely decision at the MAP and initiated the missed approach at the published point with the correct pitch, power and configuration sequence, due to the reference assessment being completed right at the point itself rather than slightly ahead of it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to complete the assessment a moment earlier so the decision is never dependent on reaching the point first.

texts_above.2: SP recognized the point at which the missed approach was due and initiated it without prompting or intervention, with the go-around started slightly late but altitude staying inside the code 2 band and no descent below MDA. Completing the reference assessment a few seconds earlier would let the decision be made exactly at the point rather than just after it. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good decision-making at minima.
texts_above.3: SP made a timely decision at the MAP, initiating the missed approach at the published point with the correct pitch, power and configuration sequence and no descent below MDA. The only refinement available is to complete the reference assessment a fraction earlier so no part of the decision trails the point itself. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good decision-making at minima.
texts_above.4: SP identified the MAP precisely and transitioned to the missed approach with negligible delay, establishing the climb and configuration in one smooth sequence with the aircraft never below MDA. There is little left to refine; the decision is already committed before the point is reached. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent decision-making at minima.

error_modes.label: Over-controlling in heading (corrections outside the heading bug width)

texts.0: SP, due to course corrections made well outside the area beneath the heading bug, over-controlled the localizer instead of damping each deviation. The corrections were reversed late and a divergent S-turn developed, taking CDI displacement past 2 dots with the trend still increasing. IP took the controls to re-establish the final approach course before the aircraft was returned to SP.
texts.1: SP, due to heading changes larger than the 5 degree limit taught for course corrections, answered every localizer deviation with an over-correction. CDI oscillated out to the 2 dot limit and remained there through two reversals until IP verbally called a specific heading to fly. SP flew the called heading and the needle recentred, with no IP control input required.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial correction taken outside the width of the heading bug, over-shot the final approach course and had to reverse the correction. CDI reached about 1.5 dots before SP reduced the input to a small specific heading change and recentred the needle. The correction was recognized and applied in time, without prompting.
texts.3: SP kept each course correction inside the 5 degree band beneath the heading bug and damped every localizer deviation on the first attempt. CDI stayed within 1 dot from the intercept to the MAP, with no reversal of correction and no oscillation. Course control required no prompting.
texts.4: SP corrected the localizer with heading changes of two to three degrees, well inside the heading bug width, removing each input before the needle passed centre. CDI remained essentially centred for the whole final segment and the aircraft tracked the course with negligible displacement. Heading control was precise and entirely unprompted.
texts.marginal: SP used corrections at the upper edge of the 5 degree band and removed them slightly late, so each deviation was answered by a small over-shoot. CDI stayed just inside 1 dot, but the reversals were growing in size as the aircraft approached MDA. Tolerance was held with a developing tendency to over-control.

texts_at.1: SP kept course corrections close to the 5 degree band beneath the heading bug, with CDI reaching close to the 2 dot limit on one correction before the reversal was applied, due to the reversal being held a beat longer than the technique calls for. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. texts_at.2: SP kept course corrections inside the 5 degree band beneath the heading bug, with CDI reaching about 1.5 dots on the first correction after intercept, due to the initial correction being taken slightly outside the bug width before it was reduced. texts_at.3: SP kept each course correction inside the 5 degree band beneath the heading bug and damped every localizer deviation, with CDI held within 1 dot from the intercept to the MAP, due to one correction sized at the upper edge of the band before it was reduced. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sound heading-correction technique.
texts_above.3: SP kept every course correction inside the 5 degree band beneath the heading bug and damped every localizer deviation on the first attempt, with CDI staying within 1 dot from the intercept to the MAP and no reversal developing. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to exceptional heading-correction technique.

error_modes.label: Drift correction not calculated and heading bug not set for the final

texts.0: SP, due to a wind corrected heading that was never calculated with the 60 to 1 rule and a heading bug left off the final approach course, flew the inbound course with no allowance for drift. The aircraft was carried downwind past 2 dots of CDI displacement and the trend continued unchecked to the MDA segment. IP intervened on the controls to regain the localizer course.
texts.1: SP, due to drift that was not determined either from the known winds or by comparing GPS track with aircraft heading, did not apply a wind correction on the final. CDI displacement built steadily downwind and stabilized at the 2 dot limit until IP verbally passed the correction to apply. The heading was then flown by SP without IP control input.
texts.2: SP, due to a drift calculation completed only after the intercept, initially flew the final on the raw inbound course. CDI opened to about 1.5 dots downwind before SP compared GPS track with heading, set the corrected value on the heading bug and recentred the needle. The correction was self-initiated and completed in time.
texts.3: SP calculated the estimated drift from the known winds and marked the wind corrected heading on the heading bug before the final approach course intercept. The bug was then used as a reference for the small corrections required and CDI stayed within 1 dot to the MAP. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP determined the drift correction before the intercept, set the wind corrected heading on the bug and flew it as the primary heading reference. The localizer needle showed only momentary displacement in the gusts and returned to centre without a heading change. Drift management was accurate and unprompted.
texts.marginal: SP calculated the drift but applied slightly less correction than the wind required, so the aircraft drifted slowly to one side of the course. CDI remained just inside 1 dot but was moving consistently in the same direction with each mile flown. Tolerance was maintained with a trend that would have opened further beyond the MDA point.

texts_at.1: SP calculated a wind corrected heading and marked it on the heading bug before the intercept, with CDI stabilizing close to the 2 dot limit downwind before the bug value was refined, due to the initial drift estimate being taken from the forecast winds rather than confirmed against GPS track. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to compare GPS track with heading immediately after intercept so the bug value is confirmed rather than assumed.
texts_at.2: SP calculated the drift and set the heading bug before the final, with CDI opening to about 1.5 dots downwind before the bug value was corrected, due to the comparison between GPS track and heading being made later than the intercept itself. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to make that comparison at the moment of intercept rather than after the drift has already shown on the needle.
texts_at.3: SP calculated the estimated drift from the known winds and marked the wind corrected heading on the bug before the final approach course intercept, with CDI held within 1 dot to the MAP, due to the bug value needing a small refinement once the actual drift in the gusts became apparent. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to plan a small buffer into the initial correction to cover the gust range expected from the forecast.

texts_above.2: SP compared GPS track with heading after CDI opened to about 1.5 dots downwind, set the corrected value on the heading bug and recentred the needle, with the correction self-initiated and completed in time. Making that comparison immediately at intercept, rather than once the drift had already shown, would keep the excursion smaller still. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid drift-correction technique.
texts_above.3: SP calculated the estimated drift from the known winds and marked the wind corrected heading on the bug before intercept, using it as the reference for corrections that held CDI within 1 dot to the MAP. The only refinement available is to build a small buffer into the initial figure for the gust range expected from the forecast. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed drift-correction technique.
texts_above.4: SP determined the drift correction before the intercept, set the wind corrected heading on the bug and flew it as the primary reference, so the needle showed only momentary displacement in the gusts, under 0.5 dot, before returning to centre. There is little left to refine; the correction is already set before the drift can show on the needle. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding drift-correction technique.

error_modes.label: Pitch changes larger than 2 degrees for descent corrections

texts.0: SP, due to pitch inputs well beyond the 2 degree limit taught for descent corrections, chased the required profile with vertical rates far above the 400 feet per minute reference. The aircraft went through the published MDA during one of the corrections and the recovery was not initiated by SP. IP intervened on the controls to arrest the descent and re-establish the aircraft at MDA.
texts.1: SP, due to descent corrections made with pitch changes greater than 2 degrees, produced vertical rates well above the 400 feet per minute reference and over-shot each correction. Altitude oscillated and the aircraft settled 200 feet above the published MDA until IP verbally called the pitch and power required. SP flew the correction with no IP control input.
texts.2: SP, due to a first descent correction taken with more than 2 degrees of pitch, generated a rate that over-shot the intended profile. The aircraft passed about 150 feet above the target altitude before SP reduced the pitch input to the taught limit and stabilized the descent. The correction was recognized and applied without prompting.
texts.3: SP limited every descent correction to approximately 2 degrees of pitch, keeping the resulting rate near the 400 feet per minute reference. The profile was flown smoothly and the aircraft was levelled within 100 feet above the published MDA with no descent below it. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP made only small pitch corrections, each well inside the 2 degree limit, so the descent rate changed gradually and the profile was flown without over-shoot. The level-off at MDA was accurate with negligible altitude excursion and no oscillation. Vertical control was precise and unprompted.
texts.marginal: SP corrected the descent with pitch inputs at the top of the 2 degree band and held them slightly long, so each correction over-shot marginally. Altitude remained within 100 feet above MDA but the excursions grew with every correction cycle. Tolerance was held with a developing tendency to chase the profile.

texts_at.1: SP limited descent corrections to close to the 2 degree pitch limit, with the aircraft settling at the 200 ft limit above the published MDA before the rate was reduced, due to the first correction of the descent being taken a fraction over the 2 degree limit before it was corrected. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to set the first correction inside the 2 degree limit rather than reducing an oversized one afterward.
texts_at.2: SP limited descent corrections to close to the 2 degree pitch limit, with the aircraft passing about 150 ft above the target altitude before the pitch input was reduced, due to the first descent correction being taken with slightly more than 2 degrees of pitch. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to check the pitch change against the attitude indicator as it is applied rather than after the rate has already built.
texts_at.3: SP limited every descent correction to approximately 2 degrees of pitch and leveled within 100 ft above the published MDA, due to one correction reaching the top of the 2 degree band before the rate stabilized. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to keep every correction in the middle of the 2 degree band rather than its upper edge.

texts_above.2: SP reduced the oversized pitch input to the taught 2 degree limit and stabilized the descent after the aircraft passed about 150 ft above the target altitude, with the correction recognized and applied without prompting. Checking the pitch change against the attitude indicator as it is applied would prevent the rate from building that far in the first place. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady pitch-correction technique.
texts_above.3: SP limited every descent correction to approximately 2 degrees of pitch, keeping the resulting rate near the reference and leveling within 100 ft above the published MDA with no descent below it. The only refinement available is to keep every correction in the middle of the 2 degree band rather than its edge. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate pitch-correction technique.
texts_above.4: SP made only small pitch corrections, each well inside the 2 degree limit, so the descent rate changed gradually and the level-off at MDA settled within about 20 ft with no oscillation. There is little left to refine; the corrections are already smaller than the limit requires. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary pitch-correction technique.

error_modes.label: Large power corrections on the final approach

texts.0: SP, due to large power corrections applied when only small adjustments from the final approach setting were required, drove the airspeed through repeated over-shoots in both directions. Airspeed excursions exceeded plus 15 and minus 10 knots from the computed final approach airspeed and the aircraft was not stabilized before MDA. IP intervened on the power lever to re-establish the approach airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to power corrections far larger than the deviation required, allowed the airspeed to over-shoot each time the throttle was moved. Airspeed reached the plus 15 knot limit from the computed final approach airspeed and stayed there until IP verbally called the torque setting for the non-precision final. The setting was made by SP with no IP control input.
texts.2: SP, due to a single oversized power correction after the FAF, over-shot the computed final approach airspeed. The excursion reached about 12 knots before SP returned to the reference torque for the configuration and allowed the speed to settle. The correction was self-initiated and completed before the profile was affected.
texts.3: SP set the power for the configured non-precision final and used only small increments to hold the computed final approach airspeed. Airspeed remained within plus 10 and minus 5 knots from the FAF to the MAP with no over-shoot after any adjustment. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP established the reference torque for the final approach configuration and thereafter used barely perceptible power adjustments. Airspeed held the computed final approach value with negligible variation through the descent and level segment. Power management was smooth and unprompted.
texts.marginal: SP used power corrections slightly larger than the deviation called for, so the airspeed over-shot marginally after each adjustment. The speed remained within plus 10 and minus 5 knots of the computed final approach airspeed but the swings increased with every correction. Tolerance was maintained with a trend towards over-controlling the power.

texts_at.1: SP set power for the configured final and used small increments, with airspeed reaching the plus 15 kt limit from the computed final approach airspeed before it was reduced, due to a single power correction being sized larger than the deviation actually required. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to size each power correction to the airspeed indication at the moment it is made rather than to habit.
texts_at.2: SP set power for the configured non-precision final, with an excursion of about 12 kt from the computed final approach airspeed before the reference torque was restored, due to a single oversized power correction after the FAF. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to check the torque setting against the reference value immediately after any power change.
texts_at.3: SP set the power for the configured non-precision final and used only small increments to hold the computed final approach airspeed within 10 kt fast and 5 kt slow, due to one increment being made a fraction larger than the deviation called for before it was trimmed back. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to keep every increment proportioned to the deviation actually showing on the indicator.

texts_above.2: SP returned to the reference torque for the configuration after an oversized power correction produced an excursion of about 12 kt, with the correction self-initiated and completed before the profile was affected. Checking the torque setting against the reference value immediately after any change would prevent the excursion from developing at all. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to dependable power-management technique.
texts_above.3: SP set the power for the configured non-precision final and used only small increments to hold the computed final approach airspeed within 10 kt fast and 5 kt slow, with no overshoot developing after any adjustment from the FAF to the MAP. The only refinement available is to proportion every increment to the deviation actually showing rather than to habit. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to notably good power-management technique.
texts_above.4: SP established the reference torque for the final approach configuration and thereafter used barely perceptible power adjustments, holding the computed final approach airspeed within about 3 kt through the descent and level segment. There is little left to refine; the adjustments are already smaller than the deviation would require. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior power-management technique.

error_modes.label: Airspeed and trim not stabilized before the FAF descent

texts.0: SP, due to configuration completed inside the 2 to 3 NM point before the FAF, began the descent with the airspeed still decaying and the aircraft out of trim. The residual control forces were not held and both airspeed and altitude diverged, with the speed passing the minus 10 knot limit while the descent profile was lost. IP intervened on the controls to re-trim and stabilize the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to gear and flap selection made too late to allow stabilization of airspeed and trim before the FAF, started the descent out of trim. The control forces were fought rather than trimmed out and the airspeed settled at the plus 15 knot limit of the computed final approach airspeed until IP verbally called for the aircraft to be trimmed. SP re-trimmed with no IP control input.
texts.2: SP, due to a configuration change completed close to the FAF, entered the descent with the trim not fully re-set. Airspeed wandered by about 12 knots from the computed final approach airspeed before SP trimmed off the control forces and re-established the reference speed. The correction was made in time and without prompting.
texts.3: SP configured the aircraft two to three miles before the FAF so that airspeed and trim were stabilized prior to the descent. The final was flown with the aircraft in trim and airspeed held within plus 10 and minus 5 knots of the computed final approach airspeed. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP completed the configuration and the Before-Landing Checklist early, trimmed the aircraft at the final approach airspeed and entered the descent hands-light. Airspeed and altitude showed negligible variation through the segment to MDA. Stabilization was accurate and entirely unprompted.
texts.marginal: SP configured only just before the 2 to 3 NM reference point and entered the descent with the trim not quite complete. Airspeed stayed within plus 10 and minus 5 knots of the computed final approach airspeed but required continuous stick pressure to hold, and the deviations grew towards MDA. Tolerance was held with a trend driven by the residual out-of-trim condition.

texts_at.1: SP configured the aircraft ahead of the FAF so airspeed and trim were close to stabilized, with airspeed settling at the plus 15 kt limit of the computed final approach airspeed before the last trim change was completed, due to the configuration being finished at the edge of the 2 to 3 NM reference point rather than ahead of it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to bring the configuration point forward so the last trim change is complete before the 2 to 3 NM point.
texts_at.2: SP configured the aircraft close to the 2 to 3 NM point, with airspeed wandering by about 12 kt from the computed final approach airspeed before the trim was completed, due to the configuration change being finished close to the reference point rather than with margin ahead of it. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to complete the trim change with enough margin that the descent starts already stabilized.
texts_at.3: SP configured the aircraft 2 to 3 NM before the FAF so that airspeed and trim were stabilized prior to the descent, holding the computed final approach airspeed within 10 kt fast and 5 kt slow, due to the trim needing one small correction as the descent began. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to check the trim a final time immediately before the descent rather than during it.

texts_above.2: SP trimmed off the residual control forces and re-established the reference speed after airspeed wandered by about 12 kt from the computed final approach airspeed, with the correction made in time and without prompting. Completing the trim change with more margin ahead of the 2 to 3 NM point would prevent the wander from developing. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured stabilization technique.
texts_above.3: SP configured the aircraft 2 to 3 NM before the FAF so airspeed and trim were stabilized prior to the descent, holding the computed final approach airspeed within 10 kt fast and 5 kt slow from the first mile of the final. The only refinement available is to check the trim a final time immediately before the descent begins. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise stabilization technique.
texts_above.4: SP completed the configuration and the Before-Landing Checklist early, trimmed the aircraft at the final approach airspeed and entered the descent hands-light, with airspeed and altitude showing variation of no more than about 2 kt through the segment to MDA. There is little left to refine; the aircraft is already stabilized well ahead of the reference point. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate stabilization technique.

error_modes.label: Descent gradient and rate from the FAF to MDA

texts.0: SP, due to a descent gradient that was not calculated for the segment from the FAF to MDA, used a rate unrelated to the distance available. The aircraft was still descending when the reference rate for the non-precision final was exceeded and it went through the published MDA before the MAP. IP intervened on the controls to stop the descent and re-establish the aircraft at the minimum altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to the descent gradient not being computed before the FAF, set a rate well below the reference for the non-precision final and arrived late on profile. The aircraft was still 200 feet above the published MDA approaching the MAP and levelled only after IP verbally called the rate required. The correction was flown by SP with no IP control input.
texts.2: SP, due to a descent rate selected without reference to the calculated gradient, descended shallower than the profile required after the FAF. The aircraft was about 150 feet high on profile before SP increased the rate towards the non-precision final reference and regained the intended descent. The correction was recognized and made in time.
texts.3: SP calculated the descent gradient for the segment inside the FAF and flew a rate close to the non-precision final reference at the torque setting for the configuration. MDA was reached in time to identify the MAP and the aircraft was levelled within 100 feet above the published minimum. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP planned the descent gradient before the FAF and flew the profile so that the aircraft arrived at MDA with adequate margin before the MAP. The rate was steady, the level-off was accurate and altitude excursions were negligible. Descent management was precise and unprompted.
texts.marginal: SP flew a rate marginally shallower than the calculated gradient required, so the profile was regained only close to the MAP. Altitude stayed within 100 feet above the published MDA but the aircraft was consistently high on the intended descent path. Tolerance was held with a trend towards arriving late at the minimum altitude.

texts_at.1: SP calculated the descent gradient for the segment inside the FAF, with the aircraft still 200 ft above the published MDA approaching the MAP before the rate was increased, due to the calculated gradient being flown at a rate slightly shallower than the reference required. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to check the actual rate against the calculated gradient earlier in the segment rather than near the MAP.
texts_at.2: SP calculated the descent gradient for the segment inside the FAF, with the aircraft about 150 ft high on profile before the rate was increased toward the reference, due to the rate being selected without a final check against the calculated gradient. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to confirm the flown rate against the calculated gradient at the start of the segment rather than partway through it.
texts_at.3: SP calculated the descent gradient for the segment inside the FAF and flew a rate close to the non-precision final reference, leveling within 100 ft above the published minimum, due to the rate needing a small increase partway through the segment to stay on the calculated profile. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to set the full calculated rate from the start of the segment rather than adjusting into it.

texts_above.2: SP increased the descent rate toward the non-precision final reference after the aircraft ran about 150 ft high on profile, regaining the intended descent path without prompting or intervention. Confirming the flown rate against the calculated gradient at the start of the segment would prevent that margin from opening. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to competent descent-planning technique.
texts_above.3: SP calculated the descent gradient for the segment inside the FAF and flew a rate close to the non-precision final reference, reaching MDA in time to identify the MAP and leveling within 100 ft above the published minimum. The only refinement available is to set the full calculated rate from the very start of the segment. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to disciplined descent-planning technique.
texts_above.4: SP planned the descent gradient before the FAF and flew the profile so the aircraft arrived at MDA with adequate margin before the MAP, with the rate constant and altitude excursions of no more than about 20 ft. There is little left to refine; the profile is already planned rather than corrected into. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to faultless descent-planning technique.

error_modes.label: Configuration and airspeed not adjusted for crosswind or gusty conditions

texts.0: SP, due to the reported gusty crosswind not being answered with the appropriate flap setting and an increased approach airspeed, flew the final at the basic configuration speed. The gusts produced excursions beyond plus 15 and minus 10 knots of the computed final approach airspeed together with course displacement past 2 dots. IP intervened on the controls to stabilize the approach.
texts.1: SP, due to the approach airspeed not being increased as required for the gusty conditions, allowed the speed to be driven by the gusts rather than by the power setting. Airspeed reached the minus 10 knot limit of the computed final approach airspeed on one gust cycle and was recovered only after IP verbally called for a higher target speed. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a gust allowance added late in the final segment, initially flew the basic approach airspeed in shifting wind. The speed varied by about 12 knots from the computed final approach airspeed before SP increased the target value and set the power accordingly. The adjustment was self-initiated and stabilized the approach.
texts.3: SP selected the appropriate flap setting for the reported crosswind and flew the final with the airspeed increased as required for the gusts. Airspeed stayed within plus 10 and minus 5 knots of the computed final approach airspeed and CDI within 1 dot to the MAP. No prompting was required.
texts.4: SP briefed the gusty crosswind, configured with the appropriate flap setting and added the required increment to the approach airspeed before the FAF. Speed and course excursions in the gusts were negligible and the aircraft remained stable to MDA. The adjustment was made accurately and without prompting.
texts.marginal: SP applied a gust allowance slightly smaller than the reported conditions justified, so each gust cycle produced a noticeable speed decay. Airspeed remained within plus 10 and minus 5 knots of the computed final approach airspeed but the excursions increased as the aircraft descended. Tolerance was maintained with a trend towards the lower limit.

texts_at.1: SP selected the appropriate flap setting for the reported crosswind and increased the approach airspeed, with the speed reaching the minus 10 kt limit on one gust cycle before the higher target was fully established, due to the gust allowance being added a beat after the first gust rather than before it. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to set the full gust allowance before the first gust is felt rather than after it.
texts_at.2: SP selected the appropriate flap setting and increased the approach airspeed for the reported conditions, with the speed varying by about 12 kt from the computed final approach airspeed before the target value was increased, due to the gust allowance being added slightly later in the final segment than the reported conditions called for. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to apply the full gust allowance at the start of the final rather than partway through it.
texts_at.3: SP selected the appropriate flap setting for the reported crosswind and flew the final with the airspeed increased as required for the gusts, holding CDI within 1 dot to the MAP, due to the increment needing a small addition once the actual gust strength became apparent. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to size the initial gust allowance from the reported peak gust rather than the mean wind.

texts_above.2: SP increased the target airspeed for the gusty conditions after the speed varied by about 12 kt from the computed final approach airspeed, with the adjustment self-initiated and stabilizing the approach. Sizing the initial allowance from the reported peak gust, rather than the mean wind, would remove the need for that adjustment. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good gust-management technique.
texts_above.3: SP selected the appropriate flap setting for the reported crosswind and flew the final with the airspeed increased as required for the gusts, holding airspeed within 10 kt fast and 5 kt slow and CDI within 1 dot to the MAP. The only refinement available is to size the initial allowance from the peak gust rather than the mean wind. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good gust-management technique.
texts_above.4: SP briefed the gusty crosswind, configured with the appropriate flap setting and added the required increment to the approach airspeed before the FAF, so speed and course excursions in the gusts stayed under about 3 kt and a quarter of a dot. There is little left to refine; the allowance is already sized before the gusts are felt. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent gust-management technique.
